Dear Sir,
Dr Adams has certainly challenged conventional
thinking with his review in the October QJM.
Cholesterol has always been a fascinating and star
subject. Some 13 scientists have been awarded
Nobel prizes for studies on cholesterol, its structure
and physiology. Brown and Goldstein in their Nobel
Prize Lecture described cholesterol as the ‘the most
highly decorated small molecule in biology’. For a
century, cholesterol studies have been characterized
by beautiful chemistry and elegant chemical analytical systems for cholesterol, lipoproteins and genetics. Atherosclerosis is a multifactorial disease, whose
aetiology may be divided into outside factors, smoking, diet, genetics, stress, viruses, etc. Circulating
blood, hormones, lipoproteins, platelets and the arterial wall whose metabolism has yet to be fully
elucidated.1
Adams suggests that alterations in the vascular
wall metabolism are important in the disease process. This could be important.2 The collagen in
joints and the colon increase their cross-linkage
with ageing, losing their elasticity, and clinical conditions result in, for example, diverticulosis.3

Presumably, the same changes in cross-linkage
occur in the collagen in the walls of blood vessels.
The deleterious effects of smoking and raised blood
pressure are unexplored as factors in elasticity
during these changes. But could these be major
pathological processes?
There are two possibilities: (i) that the cholesterol
story, despite what Dr Adams claims, is correct and
that lowering cholesterol reduces risk, and this is
now achievable pharmaceutically; or (ii) that cholesterol reduction treatment is a diversion, an expensive placebo. But by giving such treatment it enables
more important beneficial regimes to be acceptable,
i.e. stopping smoking and reducing weight.
The widespread use of statins implies the subject
is done and dusted, but Dr Adams’ note gives a
warning. It is possible that one day statins will
have their rightful place with bloodletting.
